name: Heat index
seoTitle: Heat index Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Heat index: work out heat index from the relative Humidity and the dew point. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Heat index calculator the relative Humidity and the dew point and it returns heat index. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Heat index calculator work?
sections.html:
The Heat index calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports heat index in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the relative Humidity and the dew point.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Heat index calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Heat index=(-1791 ÷ 50000 × (relative Humidity ^ 2) × (temperature ^ 2) + (36273 ÷ 5000) × (relative Humidity ^ 2) × temperature − 2956469 ÷ 18000 × (relative Humidity ^ 2) + (552933 ÷ 2500000) × relative Humidity × (temperature ^ 2) − 2922321 ÷ 200000 × relative Humidity × temperature + (420938791 ÷ 1800000) × relative Humidity − 6154047 ÷ 500000000 × (temperature ^ 2) + (161139411 ÷ 100000000) × temperature − 12353477 ÷ 1406250)
Α(T,RH)=(881 ÷ 2) × dew point ÷ (25 × dew point + 6078)
Α(T,RH)=(1 ÷ 2) × (50 × temperature × the natural log of (relative Humidity) + 881 × temperature + 12156 × the natural log of (relative Humidity)) ÷ (25 × temperature + 6078)
Heat index=((47 ÷ 18) × relative Humidity + (11 ÷ 10) × temperature − 71 ÷ 18)
Heat index=(temperature)
Heat index=(temperature, relative Humidity, (-1791 ÷ 50000 × (relative Humidity ^ 2) × (temperature ^ 2) + (36273 ÷ 5000) × (relative Humidity ^ 2) × temperature − 2956469 ÷ 18000 × (relative Humidity ^ 2) + (552933 ÷ 2500000) × relative Humidity × (temperature ^ 2) − 2922321 ÷ 200000 × relative Humidity × temperature + (420938791 ÷ 1800000) × relative Humidity − 6154047 ÷ 500000000 × (temperature ^ 2) + (161139411 ÷ 100000000) × temperature − 12353477 ÷ 1406250))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Temperature = 10 °C and Relative Humidity = 10 %. The calculator returns Dew point = -20 °C and Heat index = 16 °C.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Dew point = -20 °C and Heat index = 16 °C should be roughly the size you expected from Temperature = 10 °C and Relative Humidity = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • %, opening in percent
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Heat index calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the relative Humidity and the dew point — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Heat index calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns heat index, derived from the relative Humidity and the dew point. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Heat index calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the relative Humidity and the dew point, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Dew point = -20 °C. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Heat index calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
